cards.title: Build an Amazon FBA order forecast from marketing spend
cards.summary: Model paid orders from a monthly marketing budget divided by CAC, then layer a paid-to-organic ratio that grows as reviews accumulate.
cards.use_when: You are planning a new Amazon FBA product launch or replenishment cycle and need a 12-18 month order forecast before deciding how much inventory to buy and how much cash to raise.
steps: Set a monthly marketing budget row (example: $1,000 in month 1, $1,500 in month 2, +$1,000 each month thereafter as the business scales).
Compute paid orders per month with =ROUND(marketing budget / CAC, 0). At $1,500 spend and $41 CAC that yields 36 orders.
Add a paid-to-organic ratio that starts very low (the source uses 10%, meaning a few friends/family purchases) and rises over time. Compute organic orders as =ROUND(paid orders * ratio, 0).

Increase the ratio by a fixed step per month (source example: +10 percentage points per month) on the assumption that after roughly four to five months and ~300 orders you have accumulated enough reviews to start ranking organically.
Total orders = paid + organic, and this drives the revenue, COGS, fulfillment and inventory rows.
Freeze panes so the month header row and column labels stay visible as you scroll the model.
caveats: The 10%-per-month organic ramp and the 4-5 month review threshold are the presenter's illustrative assumptions, not measured benchmarks; tune them to your category and review velocity.
The model assumes a stable CAC; if CAC rises with spend, split the marketing row into channels.

cards.title: Model inventory timing with a lead-time lag row
cards.summary: Offset inventory purchases by the supplier lead time so the model shows when stock actually arrives and when you go negative.
cards.use_when: You are building or auditing a cash model for a physical product where stock is bought months before it can be sold.
steps: Add an inventory-purchase row for the units you pay for each month (example: 250 units at $25 = $6,300).
Add an 'inventory arrival' row that simply equals the purchase row shifted forward by the lead time — the source uses a four-month lag, so a month-2 purchase arrives in month 5.
Add a total inventory row: previous month's total inventory − units sold that month + units arriving that month.
Copy the formula across all months and hunt for negative values. A negative number means you are out of stock and cannot sell; the goal is to time purchases so total inventory never goes negative.
Use the negative months as the trigger to size the next purchase (source example: 500 units, then 1,500, then 4,000 as order volume compounds).
Multiply each purchase quantity by unit cost to get the cash outlay, and note that a 4,000-unit buy at $25 is $100,000 — this is the number that drives the financing question.
caveats: Ignore the common shortcut of expensing unit cost proportional to orders; as a founder your cash leaves in lumps, and the inventory-investment row is what reflects reality.
Lead time should include production plus freight plus inbound receiving to Amazon.

cards.title: Forecast inventory funding gaps with a monthly cash bridge
cards.summary: Separate units-sold profit from supplier-payment timing to find when an ecommerce store needs cash.
cards.use_when: You have an order and inventory forecast and need to quantify the funding gap before committing to a launch or a scaling plan.
steps: Forecast net sales and COGS for units sold; inventory purchases do not automatically become that month's COGS.
Build a cash schedule from opening cash plus customer receipts, less supplier deposits and balances, fulfillment, ads, overhead, taxes, capital spending and financing payments.
Add financing proceeds separately; reconcile closing cash to the next month's opening balance.
If starting from net income instead, adjust for non-cash items and working capital; do not subtract inventory cash twice.
Identify the lowest closing cash and add a reserve for slower sell-through, delayed payouts and higher returns.
caveats: The source's example shows months where total profit is slightly positive while cash is deeply negative — profit and cash diverge whenever you prepay inventory.
This model excludes taxes, returns and payment processing unless you add rows for them.

cards.title: Evaluate non-dilutive inventory and marketing financing
cards.summary: Revenue-share financing lets you fund inventory without selling equity, repaid as a percentage of revenue plus a flat fee.
cards.use_when: Your cash model shows a funding gap for inventory or paid acquisition and you are weighing equity dilution against revenue-based financing.
steps: Identify the peak cash gap from inventory lead times and acquisition plans.
Compare financing offers on total cost, repayment timing, collateral, covenants and downside cash exposure, alongside equity alternatives.
Keep inventory payments in the cash schedule and add cash financing proceeds separately. If the lender pays suppliers directly, reconcile the financed purchase without inventing a cash receipt.
Model principal, fees and revenue-linked payments separately; do not delete inventory costs or treat financing as revenue.
Stress-test slower sales and margin compression against the repayment schedule.
Obtain current provider quotes; the source's historical rates and program names are not current offers.
caveats: Revenue-based funding can strain cash even when accounting profit is positive.
Non-dilutive describes ownership, not absence of borrowing cost or risk.

cards.title: Calculate customer lifetime value from churn and gross margin
cards.summary: Estimate subscription contribution LTV using consistent monthly purchase frequency, margin and churn, then validate against observed cohorts.
cards.use_when: You are setting a CAC ceiling for a subscription or repeat-purchase store and need to know how much you can afford to spend to acquire one customer.
steps: Use monthly orders per active customer, net AOV, explicitly defined contribution rate and monthly customer churn.
Under constant monthly churn c, expected billed periods are approximately 1/c for customers active at the first bill.
Illustration: $25 AOV x 60% contribution x 1.35 orders per active month / 22% monthly churn = about $92 contribution LTV.
A $92 CAC would consume all modeled lifetime contribution before overhead, time value and risk; set a lower ceiling with a payback constraint.
Check monthly cohort cash contribution and observed repeat orders; do not apply subscription churn mechanically to non-subscription purchases.
caveats: LTV is most important for subscription or repeat-purchase businesses; it matters less for one-time-purchase categories.
The formula is only as good as the churn assumption — using an early, high-churn cohort understates LTV, and a mature cohort may overstate it for new traffic.

cards.title: Spend above first-order profit when LTV justifies it
cards.summary: A subscription can profitably spend more on acquisition than the first order returns because later months repay the CAC.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to scale paid acquisition on a subscription product even though first-order economics look unprofitable.
steps: Compute first-order contribution: AOV × gross margin (example: $25 × 60% = $15) versus your CAC.
If CAC is higher than first-order contribution, check whether cumulative gross profit across the average lifetime exceeds CAC.
Use the cohort view: month 0 has 986 transactions, month 1 has 986 × (1 − churn), and each month's revenue × gross margin accumulates.
In the source's example, even spending $50 to acquire a customer whose first order only nets $15 works, because the average 4.5-month lifetime repays it and adds profit.
For hyper-growth planning, use historical churn rates to predict the payback period (the source cites roughly one year to profitability at very high growth rates) before committing ad budget.
Investors evaluating the business will ask for LTV before funding growth spend — keep the cohort calculation current.
caveats: This only works if churn is stable and measured; if churn worsens as you scale into colder traffic, the payback promise breaks.
The example numbers are illustrative, not benchmarks.

cards.title: Model discounts and CAC as one combined acquisition cost
cards.summary: A discount and paid acquisition are mathematically equivalent spend per customer — add them together to see true cost of acquisition.
cards.use_when: You are choosing between a deeper discount and more ad spend to drive first purchases and want to compare them on equal footing.
steps: Define the unit economics of one customer: net AOV (after discount) − COGS = contribution margin; then subtract CAC = contribution margin post-marketing.
Run a scenario table with identical ad spend across scenarios (source example: $100,000 each, $1.50 per click, 66,667 sessions, $200 list price, $75 COGS).
Vary the discount (0%, $30, $60) and set an assumed conversion-rate lift for each (source's illustrative assumptions: 1.5% → 2.2% → 3.8%).
Compute purchases, CAC (= ad spend ÷ purchases) and contribution margin post-marketing for each scenario.

In the source's example all three scenarios land at exactly $25 contribution margin post-marketing per customer because discount + CAC totalled $100 in each — the discount is not automatically worse than the ad spend.
Use this to decide allocation: the discount and the ad budget are two ways to spend the same acquisition dollar, and the split is a choice, not a fixed rule.
caveats: The conversion lifts and $100 discount+CAC equality are the presenter's constructed example, not a universal result — real conversion lift depends on your price point, audience and offer.
Discount depth can damage brand perception and reference prices over time; the source cautions against discounting indiscriminately.

cards.title: Choose the discount/CAC mix that maximises total contribution margin
cards.summary: Compare scenarios on total revenue and total post-marketing contribution margin, not on per-customer margin alone.
cards.use_when: You are setting a promotional calendar or ad budget and deciding whether a bigger discount can be offset by higher volume.
steps: For each scenario multiply purchases × net AOV to get net sales, and purchases × COGS for total COGS.
Subtract total COGS and total ad spend from net sales to get total post-marketing contribution margin.
In the source's worked example: no discount returns $25,000; $30 off returns $36,000; $60 off returns $63,000 on the same $100,000 ad spend.
Compare this against the opposite strategy: shrinking revenue on a smaller set of customers can also maximise profit if per-customer unit economics are exceptional. There is no universal winner.
Choose the scenario with the highest total contribution margin subject to your brand and capacity constraints.
caveats: Source-specific example numbers; your conversion elasticity to discount depth may be much flatter or steeper.
Deeper discounts that attract discount-only buyers can raise future churn and erode base-price demand.

cards.title: Attach your best discounts to a loyalty or subscription on-ramp
cards.summary: Give the deepest discounts in exchange for enrolling in a subscription or loyalty program rather than as a flash sale.
cards.use_when: You are designing the offer and landing page for a promotion and deciding whether the discount should require a commitment.
steps: Instead of a pure flash sale, structure the best discount as the entry point into a subscription or loyalty program.
Rationale: flash-sale buyers often will not buy again without another large discount, while a customer who accepts a subscription has self-selected into higher lifetime value.
Reserve the biggest discount for the customers most likely to stay; do not spread the deepest discounts across one-time transactional traffic.
Budget the discount and the ad spend out of one pool for the year (source example: $5M to zero) and split it between discounts and marketing based on which produces more sales lift.
Whoever runs marketing should own the combined pool, since both levers have the same profit impact per dollar.
caveats: The equivalence between discount dollars and ad dollars holds at the point of acquisition; the downstream retention effect differs by which lever you used, which is exactly why the on-ramp matters.
The $5M pool figure is the presenter's illustration of a single budget construct.
